title: Christ, first in God's plan
hookLine: Franciscan thinkers held Christ would have come even without sin; others disagree

lines: WHAT IF NO ONE HAD SINNED?
cards: Here's a question with no way to check the answer. Suppose Adam and Eve had never sinned. Would there still have been a Christmas?

It sounds like a question for a sleepless night, but medieval teachers took it seriously, because the answer says something about why Christ came at all. Was he God's rescue plan, sent because things went wrong?
Or was he the plan from the beginning? Today, two honest answers.

teach.h: AQUINAS: HE CAME BECAUSE OF SIN.
teach.b: Start with Thomas Aquinas. He notices that whenever Scripture gives a reason for the Son of God becoming man, the reason is sin: he came to save.

So, Aquinas says, it's more fitting to say that if humanity had not sinned, the Incarnation would not have happened. And he adds a careful line: God's power isn't limited by that. God could have done it anyway.
The Church sings something close to this view at the Easter Vigil, in a hymn that calls Adam's sin a happy fault, because it won so great a Redeemer. Now Duns Scotus, the Franciscan, from yesterday.
He comes at it from love, not from the problem. God, he says, does things in order. When you plan a house, you think of the house first and the bricks after.
God's first and highest intention, the thing all of creation is for, is Christ: the Son joined to a human nature, the masterpiece of God's love. Everything else is willed for his sake.
So Christ wasn't a patch for a broken plan. He was the plan. Sin changed the way he came, as a Redeemer who suffered.

But he would have come. Scotus leans on Paul's letter to the Colossians, in the Douay-Rheims: "Who is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature: For in him were all things created."
Franciscan thinkers after Scotus took this up as their own.
Both answers are held by Catholics, and the Church hasn't chosen between them.
One sees Christ as the rescuer who came because we fell. The other sees him as the reason there was a world to fall in.

how: Catholics are free to hold either view on why the Son of God became man; theologians in the line of Scotus teach the primacy of Christ, and theologians in the line of Aquinas teach that the Incarnation was willed as the remedy for sin.

o: the family surname of Jesus of Nazareth
for Scotus, God's first intention, not a backup plan
a title Scotus gave to Adam before his fall

s: the Church has settled the question and ruled Scotus wrong
both answers are held by Catholics, and the Church hasn't chosen between them.
Aquinas said God could not have become man without sin
he said it was more fitting to say so, but that God's power isn't limited by it.
Scotus thought sin changed the way Christ came, but not whether he came
for Scotus, Christ was willed first; sin made him come as a suffering Redeemer.

games.q: you're Duns Scotus. someone asks whether the Son of God would have become man if no one had ever sinned. what do you answer?
o: no; he came only to fix what went wrong.
yes; Christ was God's first intention, sin or no sin.
no one can say anything about it.
games.why: Scotus says Christ was willed first, the masterpiece of God's love. Aquinas leaned the other way, and the Church allows both.

practice: Hold the two pictures side by side: in one, the world goes wrong and Christ comes to set it right; in the other, the world was made with Christ in mind from the start. Notice which one your mind leans toward, then let both rest.
If you pray, simply thank God for Christ, however the plan was drawn; if you don't, stay with the question and the breath.

wordCard.voice: Christ. For Scotus and those who followed him, not God's backup plan but the first thing God willed, the firstborn of every creature. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: the anointed one, the New Testament's word for the Hebrew Messiah.

carryVoice: Your line: christ first. Two answers, both held, and the Church asks no one to pick. Back tomorrow, same hill.
